prompt: `-rw-r----- 1 ana team report.md`. Bruno is in `team` and is not ana. What may he do?
hint: Work out which of the three rows applies to him, then read it.

choices.text: Read and write it, since he shares the group
choices.why: The group's three characters are `r--`. There is no w in them.

choices.text: Neither, since the last three characters are dashes
choices.why: Those apply to people in neither role. He is in the group.

choices.text: Read it
choices.why: Right: the group row is `r--`, and that is his row.

choices.text: Read it, and delete it if he owns the directory
choices.why: Deleting depends on the directory, and that was not stated here.

prompt: A file is `-r--rwxrwx`, owned by ana, group team. Ana is in team. She runs `echo x >> file` and is refused. Why?
hint: Three rows, and the checking stops somewhere.

choices.text: The group row needs the owner's row to agree as well
choices.why: The rows are independent. One of them is chosen, and the others are not consulted.

choices.text: The owner's row is checked first, and it says r--
choices.why: Right. Being in the group as well buys her nothing once her own row has matched.

choices.text: A file that is writable by everybody is protected from its owner
choices.why: No such rule exists. The mode was chosen deliberately to produce this.

choices.text: She needs to be in the group's primary position for the group row to count
choices.why: Supplementary membership counts for the group row. Her own row was reached first.

prompt: Carla is in neither the owner's account nor the file's group. Which characters apply to her?
hint: Count from the end.

choices.text: The first three
choices.why: Those are the owner's.

choices.text: The middle three
choices.why: Those are the group's, and she is in neither role named so far.

choices.text: The union of the three rows
choices.why: Rows are not combined. One is selected.

choices.text: The last three
choices.why: Right — `other` is what is left when the first two do not match.

prompt: You can delete a file you cannot read and do not own. What makes that possible?
hint: Removing a name is a change to a list.

choices.text: Write permission on the directory holding it
choices.why: Right, and it is why /tmp needs the extra bit from section 63.

choices.text: Write permission on the file itself
choices.why: Writing a file changes its contents; removal is a different operation.

choices.text: Being in the same group as the file
choices.why: The group decides what its three characters say, and removal is not there.

choices.text: The file having no links left pointing at it
choices.why: That is a consequence of removal rather than a condition for it.

prompt: How many characters does a long listing show before the link count, and what is the first one?
hint: People count nine and find one more.

choices.text: Nine, and the first is the owner's read bit
choices.why: There are ten, and the first is not a permission at all.

choices.text: Ten, and the first is the type
choices.why: Right: type, then three rows of three.

choices.text: Twelve, and the first three are the special bits
choices.why: The special bits share the x slots rather than having their own.

choices.text: Ten, and the first is the owner's execute bit
choices.why: Execute sits third in the owner's row, not in front of it.

prompt: A symlink always lists as `lrwxrwxrwx`. Is that a security problem?
hint: Ask which file's permissions are consulted when you open it.

choices.text: Yes — anybody may rewrite where it points
choices.why: Rewriting the link needs write permission on the directory, not on the link.

choices.text: Yes, unless the target is also world-writable
choices.why: The target's own mode is the one that governs, whatever the link says.

choices.text: No — the target's permissions are what get checked
choices.why: Right: a symlink's own bits are never consulted on open.

choices.text: No, because the kernel refuses to follow a world-writable link
choices.why: It follows it. The check happens at the target.

prompt: `namei -l` on a path prints a line per step. What question does it answer that `ls -l` does not?
hint: A file is reached through directories.

choices.text: Whether each directory lets you through
choices.why: Right, and that is the cause of a denial about half the time.

choices.text: Whether the file is a symlink to somewhere else
choices.why: It shows that too, and `ls -l` shows it just as clearly.

choices.text: Which user and group own the file
choices.why: Both commands print that, on the file's own line.

choices.text: What the file's size and modification time are
choices.why: Neither of those appears in namei's output.

prompt: A listing shows `-rwSr--r--`. What is wrong with it?
hint: A capital in an x slot says two things at once.

choices.text: It is fine: capital S is how setuid is drawn
choices.why: Lowercase s is setuid with execute. The capital means something else.

choices.text: The file is a socket rather than an ordinary file
choices.why: A socket shows `s` as the first character, which is a different position.

choices.text: The owner is shut out of reading it
choices.why: The owner's row starts `rw`, so reading is fine.

choices.text: setuid is on and execute is off
choices.why: Right, and a setuid program nobody may run does nothing at all.

prompt: Which character at the end of a mode in `ls -l` means the file carries an access control list?
hint: One character, and it is not a letter.

prompt: Write `-rw-r--r--` as three octal digits.
hint: Read 4, write 2, execute 1, added up per group of three.

prompt: Write `640` as the nine permission characters, with no leading type character.
hint: Six is read plus write; four is read; zero is nothing.

prompt: Why are permissions written in base 8 rather than base 10?
hint: Count the bits in one group.

choices.text: Because Unix predates decimal notation in system tools
choices.why: Decimal is older than Unix by some centuries.

choices.text: Because three bits hold a value from 0 to 7
choices.why: Right, and one octal digit is exactly three bits.

choices.text: Because there are eight permission bits in total
choices.why: There are nine, plus three special ones.

choices.text: Because base 8 avoids the ambiguity of letters in hexadecimal
choices.why: Hexadecimal would fit three rows in fewer digits, and the grouping would stop lining up.

prompt: `chmod 755` is run on a file whose mode was `4755`. What happens to the setuid bit?
hint: A three-digit number is a four-digit number with a zero in front.

choices.text: It is cleared
choices.why: Right — and that is how a working setuid program quietly stops working.

choices.text: It is kept, since three digits describe just the nine bits
choices.why: Three digits set the fourth to zero. Symbolic form is what leaves it alone.

choices.text: It is kept, and a warning is printed
choices.why: chmod says nothing at all here.

choices.text: The command is refused, because the modes have different widths
choices.why: It is accepted. Both are valid ways of stating a mode.

prompt: A forum answer says to fix a permission problem with `chmod 777`. What is the objection?
hint: Ask what it fixed and what it stopped checking.

choices.text: It is slower than setting the bits individually
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: It works, and it has to be repeated after each reboot
choices.why: Modes are stored on disk and survive a reboot.

choices.text: There is no way back once it has been applied
choices.why: chmod goes both ways; the objection is about what it leaves behind.

choices.text: It removes the check instead of the cause
choices.why: Right, and whatever was actually wrong is still wrong, along with everything else.

prompt: You downloaded a script and want to run it. Which form changes the least?
hint: One of these states the whole mode and the other adds one bit.

choices.text: chmod 755 script.sh
choices.why: That works, and it also rewrites the other eight bits.

choices.text: chmod 777 script.sh
choices.why: That works, and it opens the file to everybody on the machine.

choices.text: chmod +x script.sh
choices.why: Right — one bit added, nothing else touched.

choices.text: chmod a=rwx script.sh
choices.why: The equals sign clears whatever the rows held before it.

prompt: `chmod -R 644 .` was run inside a project directory and now nothing in it can be reached. What went wrong?
hint: Files and directories want different bits from the same number.

choices.text: 644 is not a valid mode for a directory and chmod rejected it
choices.why: It was accepted; the result is what caused the trouble.

choices.text: The command changed ownership as well as the mode
choices.why: chmod touches the mode. Ownership is chown's job.

choices.text: Recursion reached a mount point and changed another filesystem
choices.why: One filesystem was involved, and the mode is the whole story.

choices.text: The directories lost their x, so nothing could enter them
choices.why: Right, and `chmod -R u+rwX,go+rX` is the repair, because capital X spares plain files.

prompt: In `chmod -R u+rwX,go+rX tree/`, what does the capital `X` do that a lowercase `x` would not?
hint: It looks at what the entry already is.

choices.text: It spares plain files that lack it
choices.why: Right, which is why a text file in the tree stays non-executable.

choices.text: It grants execute and clears the other two bits
choices.why: That is what the equals sign does. X only ever adds.

choices.text: It grants execute just to the entries you happen to own
choices.why: Who it applies to is the `u` and `go` in front, not the X.

choices.text: It grants execute and marks the entry setuid
choices.why: Setuid is `s`, and it is a different letter for a different bit.

prompt: Bruno is in a file's group and can read it. `chmod g+w` on it is refused with `Operation not permitted`. Why?
hint: Changing a mode is a different right from using it.

choices.text: He would need write permission on the file first
choices.why: Even with w he could not change the mode; that right belongs elsewhere.

choices.text: That right belongs to the owner and to root
choices.why: Right, and letting the group do it would make the model meaningless.

choices.text: The file sits on a filesystem mounted without write access
choices.why: Then the message would name the filesystem instead.

choices.text: His group membership has not taken effect in this session
choices.why: It has — he read the file a moment earlier.

prompt: Write the chmod that makes a file readable and writable by its owner, readable by its group, and invisible to everybody else — using three octal digits.
hint: Six, four, zero.

prompt: What does `x` grant on a directory?
hint: A directory is a list of names, and the letters are permissions on that list.

choices.text: Permission to run the files inside it
choices.why: Each file carries its own execute bit for that.

choices.text: Permission to see the names it holds
choices.why: That is what `r` grants.

choices.text: Permission to go through it
choices.why: Right — traverse, and the usual word for it is search.

choices.text: Permission to create and remove entries in it
choices.why: That is `w`, and it is a separate bit.

prompt: A directory is `dr--r--r--`. `ls` on it works and `cat dir/file.txt` is refused. Why?
hint: Two separate bits answer two separate questions.

choices.text: Listing needs r, and reaching a file needs x
choices.why: Right: you get the names and cannot walk through to what they point at.

choices.text: The file inside has no read permission for you
choices.why: Its mode is 644, and the directory is what refused.

choices.text: cat needs execute on the file it opens
choices.why: Reading a file needs r on the file. Execute is for running it.

choices.text: The directory is missing its w, so reading is incomplete
choices.why: w is about adding and removing entries, and reading does neither.

prompt: A directory is `d--x--x--x`. What can somebody who is not the owner do with it?
hint: Reverse the previous case.

choices.text: See the list of names, without opening any of them
choices.why: That is the r-without-x case, and this is its opposite.

choices.text: Add files to it, without reading any of them back
choices.why: Adding needs w, which is absent here.

choices.text: Neither read nor write nor traverse: the bits are useless
choices.why: One bit is present, and it is the one that does the most.

choices.text: Open a file inside, given the name
choices.why: Right, and that is how a home directory set to 711 works.

prompt: `readable.txt` is `-rw-r--r--` and sits in a directory that is `drwx------` owned by somebody else. Can you read it?
hint: A path is walked one directory at a time.

choices.text: Yes — the file's own mode grants it to everybody
choices.why: Its mode is generous and unreachable, which is the same as no.

choices.text: No — you cannot get through the directory to reach it
choices.why: Right, and `namei -l` prints exactly which step refused.

choices.text: Yes, if you use the full absolute path rather than a relative one
choices.why: Both walk the same directories, and both stop at the same one.

choices.text: No, because a file inherits the directory's mode when it is created
choices.why: It does not inherit it; the two modes are independent, and the walk is what fails.

prompt: Match each directory mode to what it lets a stranger do.
hint: Two of the four grant exactly one useful thing.

pairs.right: list it and pass through it
reach a file by name, see no list

right_distractors: remove any entry, including other people's
create entries that inherit the group

prompt: `ls -ln` prints numbers where `ls -l` printed names. Which of the two is closer to what the filesystem stores?
hint: Names have to be looked up somewhere.

choices.text: ls -l, because names are what the inode records
choices.why: The inode records numbers; the names are resolved for display.

choices.text: Neither — both are computed from the same stored string
choices.why: One is stored and one is looked up.

choices.text: ls -l, because the numbers are derived from the names
choices.why: The derivation runs the other way.

choices.text: ls -ln, because owner and group are stored as numbers
choices.why: Right, and it is why a disk moved between machines can change hands.

prompt: Ana owns a file and is in the group `team`. `chown bruno file` is refused and `chgrp team file` works. What separates them?
hint: One of the two hands the file to somebody else.

choices.text: chgrp is a shell builtin and chown is a program
choices.why: Both are programs in /usr/bin.

choices.text: chgrp changes fewer bytes in the inode
choices.why: Both write one field, and size is not the criterion.

choices.text: Giving a file away needs root
choices.why: Right, and the reason is quotas: you could otherwise charge your files to a colleague.

choices.text: chown was refused because bruno has no home directory
choices.why: Whether bruno has a home is irrelevant to owning a file.

prompt: A deploy runs `sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /srv/www` and the service still cannot read a file there. What was not changed?
hint: Ownership and permission are two separate fields.

choices.text: The mode, which chown leaves exactly as it was
choices.why: Right: ownership and permission are separate fields, and a 600 file or a directory without x still refuses.

choices.text: The group, which chown leaves alone when given two names
choices.why: Two names separated by a colon set both.

choices.text: The file's inode, which keeps the previous owner
choices.why: The inode is exactly what was rewritten.

choices.text: The parent directory, which chown left out of the walk
choices.why: -R descends; the parent itself was the argument.

prompt: Write the command that sets a file's owner to `ana` and its group to `team` in one go, on `report.md`.
hint: One command, one colon.

prompt: `id` prints `gid=1002(ana)` and `groups=1002(ana),27(sudo),1004(team)`. What is the gid line for?
hint: One of the memberships has a job the others do not.

choices.text: It is the group with the lowest number, listed first
choices.why: Ordering is incidental. The gid line names a role rather than a position.

choices.text: It is the primary group, which new files get
choices.why: Right, and the rest count for permission checks just as much.

choices.text: It is the group that grants elevated rights
choices.why: That is whichever group the sudoers file names, and it is a separate question.

choices.text: It is the group the account was created with, kept for history
choices.why: It is live, not historical: it decides the group of everything you create.

prompt: `sudo usermod -aG deploy ana` succeeds, `getent group deploy` shows her, and `id -nG` in her shell does not. Why?
hint: Ask when a process learns its group list.

choices.text: usermod writes the change at the next reboot
choices.why: The file was written immediately, which is why getent already sees it.

choices.text: id reads a cache that refreshes once in a quarter hour
choices.why: id asks the kernel about the current process, and there is no such cache.

choices.text: The shell predates the change
choices.why: Right: groups are attached at process start and inherited, so a fresh login is the fix.

choices.text: The group needs a gid below 1000 to be picked up
choices.why: Numbers under 1000 are a convention for system groups, and nothing here depends on it.

prompt: What does the `-a` in `usermod -aG team bruno` prevent?
hint: Think about what the command does to his other memberships.

choices.text: Replacing the list with the one group named
choices.why: Right, and leaving it out is the usual way somebody loses access to sudo.

choices.text: Changing his primary group as a side effect
choices.why: Primary is -g, and -G touches the supplementary list.

choices.text: Creating the group if it does not exist
choices.why: usermod refuses an absent group either way; groupadd is what creates one.

choices.text: Prompting for confirmation before writing /etc/group
choices.why: It writes without asking in both forms, which is part of why -a matters.

prompt: Somebody is put in the `docker` group so they can run containers. What has effectively been granted?
hint: Ask what a container can be told to mount.

choices.text: Read access to the container images, and that is the extent of it
choices.why: Images are the least of it; the daemon can do considerably more on request.

choices.text: The right to run containers under their own account, and no other
choices.why: The daemon runs them, and the daemon is root.

choices.text: A limited, audited subset of root, like a narrow sudoers rule
choices.why: Nothing narrows it: the request goes to a root daemon that honours it.

choices.text: Root, in practice
choices.why: Right, and it is the same decision as granting sudo, usually made as though it were not.

prompt: Which command prints the names of every group you belong to, and nothing else?
hint: Two words, and the second is a capital letter after a dash.

prompt: With a umask of `022`, what mode does a newly created file get?
hint: Programs ask for 666, and the mask takes bits away.

choices.why: That is the request, before the mask is applied.
That is what a new directory gets, because directories are requested as 777.
Right: 666 with the group's and other's write bits removed.
That is the result under a umask of 077.

prompt: Why is a newly created shell script never executable, whatever the umask?
hint: A mask removes and does not add.

choices.text: Because the shell strips the execute bit from files it creates
choices.why: The shell does nothing of the kind; the request never contained the bit.

choices.text: Because nothing asked for execute in the first place
choices.why: Right — files are requested as 666, and a mask of 000 still gives 666.

choices.text: Because execute is granted by the filesystem at mount time
choices.why: A mount option can forbid it; nothing grants it per file at mount.

choices.text: Because a script is data until an interpreter claims it
choices.why: The bit is what decides, and a compiled program would be in the same position.

prompt: A service writes files with the wrong permissions. You set `umask 027` in your `~/.bashrc` and it changes nothing. Why?
hint: Ask what started the service.

choices.text: A umask in a dotfile applies at the next reboot
choices.why: It applies to the next shell you open, and to nothing else.

choices.text: 027 is invalid as a umask and was ignored
choices.why: It is a perfectly ordinary umask; the problem is where it was set.

choices.text: The service already created the files, so the mask came too late
choices.why: It writes new ones constantly, and they come out the same way.

choices.text: The service is started by systemd, which has its own
choices.why: Right, and `UMask=` in the unit file is where it belongs.

prompt: `chmod +x file` under a umask of `077` grants execute to the owner alone. Why is `chmod a+x` different?
hint: One of the two names its audience.

choices.text: A bare +x is filtered by the umask; a+x states who and is not
choices.why: Right, and it is a good reason to write the audience out every time.

choices.text: a+x sets the special bits as well as the nine
choices.why: Special bits are s and t, and neither is involved here.

choices.text: chmod refuses a bare +x on a file with no execute bit set
choices.why: It accepts it, and the result is what differs.

choices.text: The umask applies to directories and a+x forces the file case
choices.why: The mask applies to both, and the filtering here is about the missing audience.

prompt: Which umask gives new files 600 and new directories 700?
hint: Three digits, and the last two are the same.

prompt: `/usr/bin/passwd` is `-rwsr-xr-x`, owned by root. What does the `s` do when you run it?
hint: The file it has to write is readable by root alone.

choices.text: It keeps the program resident in memory between runs
choices.why: That was the sticky bit's original meaning, on a different system, decades ago.

choices.text: It makes the program ask for your password before starting
choices.why: The program asks because it was written to; the bit is about identity.

choices.text: The process takes on the file's owner
choices.why: Right, which is how you edit a file owned by root without being root.

choices.text: It grants you read access to /etc/shadow for the session
choices.why: Your access is unchanged; the process is what runs as somebody else.

prompt: `/srv/team` is `drwxrwsr-x`, group `team`. Bruno's primary group is `bruno`. What group does a file he creates there get?
hint: The s is in the group slot of a directory.

choices.text: team
choices.why: Right — setgid on a directory makes new entries inherit its group.

choices.text: bruno
choices.why: That is what it would be without the bit, and it is what the bit exists to avoid.

choices.text: root, since root owns the directory
choices.why: Ownership of the directory sets the owner of nothing inside it.

choices.text: Whichever group his umask selects
choices.why: A umask decides bits; it has no opinion about which group.

prompt: `/tmp` is `drwxrwxrwt`. Bruno has write permission on it. Why is he refused when he deletes ana's file there?
hint: The last character is doing the work.

choices.text: Her file is 644, so he lacks write permission on it
choices.why: Deleting is governed by the directory, and 644 would be no obstacle without the last character.

choices.text: The file is open in another process
choices.why: Deleting an open file succeeds; the name goes and the data waits.

choices.text: He is not in her group
choices.why: Group membership decides the file's middle row, and deletion is not decided there.

choices.text: The last character restricts removal
choices.why: Right, and without it a world-writable /tmp would be unusable.

prompt: You are about to make a shell script setuid root so a colleague can run it. What should you do instead?
hint: Linux has an opinion about setuid scripts already.

choices.text: Wrap it in a compiled binary and set the bit on that
choices.why: That moves the vulnerability rather than removing it; the script still runs as root.

choices.text: Write a narrow sudoers rule naming that one command
choices.why: Right, and it is logged and revocable, which the bit is not.

choices.text: Put the script in a directory owned by root and set 4755 on the directory
choices.why: setuid on a directory does nothing at all on Linux.

choices.text: Give the colleague ownership of the script and leave the bit off
choices.why: That lets them edit it, and it does not give them the access they needed.

prompt: Write the four-digit octal mode of a world-writable directory that is safe to share, like `/tmp`.
hint: Seven seven seven, with one digit in front.

prompt: What is special about uid 0?
hint: It is simpler and more absolute than people expect.

choices.text: It belongs to each group the machine has
choices.why: Its group list is short; membership is not the mechanism.

choices.text: Its files are created with mode 777
choices.why: root's umask applies like anybody's.

choices.text: Its permission bits count as set, file by file
choices.why: The bits are not consulted at all, which is stronger.

choices.text: The kernel skips the permission check for it
choices.why: Right — there is no check to pass rather than a check that passes.

prompt: `su -` on a fresh Ubuntu machine fails no matter what you type. What is going on?
hint: The account it is asking about has been dealt with deliberately.

choices.text: su has been removed from the distribution
choices.why: It is installed and running; it is the answer that fails.

choices.text: The root account has no password set
choices.why: Right, which is a deliberate choice: the distribution wants you to use sudo.

choices.text: su requires a terminal that reports as a login shell
choices.why: The dash makes it a login shell, and that is not what refused.

choices.text: Your account is missing from the sudoers file
choices.why: su does not consult sudoers at all; that is sudo's file.

prompt: Carla types her correct password and gets `carla is not in the sudoers file`. What did sudo do, in what order?
hint: It said two different things, and one of them was about identity.

choices.text: It refused her before asking, and the prompt was cosmetic
choices.why: The prompt was real: it checked the password against her account.

choices.text: It matched her against the file and then verified the password
choices.why: The order runs the other way, and it matters for what an attacker learns.

choices.text: It authenticated her, then found no rule that applies to her
choices.why: Right — confirm who you are, then say what you are not allowed to do.

choices.text: It compared her password against root's and found no match
choices.why: sudo asks for your own password, not root's; that is su's model.

prompt: Why edit `/etc/sudoers` with `visudo` rather than with an editor directly?
hint: Think about what a syntax error costs on a machine where root has no password.

choices.text: visudo checks the syntax before saving
choices.why: Right, and a broken sudoers on a passwordless-root machine is a rescue-disk afternoon.

choices.text: visudo encrypts the file, which a plain editor would corrupt
choices.why: The file is plain text; nothing about it is encrypted.

choices.text: visudo is the one editor permitted to write files owned by root
choices.why: Any editor under sudo writes root's files.

choices.text: visudo reloads the rules, which an editor leaves stale
choices.why: The rules are read on each invocation, so no reload exists to forget.

prompt: Which command prints the list of things sudo will let you run on this machine?
hint: Two words, and the second is a single letter after a dash.

prompt: `sudo echo x > /root/marker.txt` fails with `bash: /root/marker.txt: Permission denied`. Who refused?
hint: Read the first word of the message.

choices.text: sudo, because writing under /root needs an explicit rule
choices.why: sudo never spoke; the line names bash.

choices.text: echo, which refuses to write outside your home directory
choices.why: echo writes to its own output and knows nothing about paths.

choices.text: The kernel, which blocks redirects into root-owned directories
choices.why: The kernel refused a write, and it refused it to bash rather than to a redirect rule.

choices.text: Your own shell, which opened the file before sudo ran
choices.why: Right — the redirect belongs to the shell, and the shell is still you.

prompt: Which of these writes a line into a root-owned file and shows you what it wrote?
hint: One of them runs a program that opens the file itself.

choices.text: echo 'line' | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
choices.why: Right: tee opens the file, tee is under sudo, and it echoes the content back.

choices.text: sudo echo 'line' >> /etc/hosts 2>/dev/null
choices.why: The redirect is the shell's, and the shell is not root.

choices.text: sudo cat 'line' >> /etc/hosts
choices.why: cat would look for a file called line, and the redirect is still the shell's.

choices.text: echo 'line' >> sudo /etc/hosts
choices.why: That is not a command; sudo would be read as a filename.

prompt: A program you installed in `~/bin` works at your prompt and is `command not found` under sudo. Why?
hint: sudo replaces something before it looks.

choices.text: sudo refuses to run programs from a home directory
choices.why: It runs what it finds; the question is where it looked.

choices.text: The program lost its execute bit when you elevated
choices.why: Bits are on disk and do not change per invocation.

choices.text: secure_path replaced your PATH with a fixed one
choices.why: Right, and the fix is the full path, or a directory on that list.

choices.text: env_reset cleared the program's own environment variables
choices.why: env_reset is real and clears variables; finding the program is PATH's job.

prompt: What is the objection to `curl https://example.com/install.sh | sudo bash`?
hint: Ask what you have read before it runs as root.

choices.text: It is slower than downloading and running the file
choices.why: Speed is beside the point, and the pipe is if anything faster.

choices.text: Nobody has read the script that is about to run as root
choices.why: Right, and it is the most successful delivery mechanism there is on Linux.

choices.text: bash refuses to read a script from standard input
choices.why: It reads standard input happily, which is part of why this pattern spread.

choices.text: curl drops the exit status, so a failed download still runs
choices.why: That is a real flaw in the pattern, and it is the smaller of the two.

prompt: You forgot the sudo on the previous command. Write the two characters that stand for that command so you can prefix it.
hint: Two of the same character.

prompt: What problem do ACLs solve that owner-group-other cannot?
hint: Count how many named parties the nine bits can describe.

choices.text: Permissions that change with the time of day
choices.why: Neither mechanism knows what time it is.

choices.text: Permissions that follow a process instead of a person
choices.why: That is what SELinux and AppArmor are for.

choices.text: A second named person, and nobody else
choices.why: Right: one owner and one group is the limit the nine bits have.

choices.text: Permissions that survive a file being copied
choices.why: Copying drops them unless the tool is told to keep them.

prompt: A tree depends on ACLs and a backup restores it without them. What was skipped?
hint: Two common tools drop them by default.

choices.text: The filesystem was mounted without ACL support during the restore
choices.why: Possible, and the usual cause is simpler and on the tool's command line.

choices.text: The ACLs expired, as they carry a validity period
choices.why: They have no such thing; they sit in the file's extended attributes.

choices.text: The restore ran as root, which ignores them
choices.why: root ignoring them changes what root may do, not what is written back.

choices.text: `cp` needs `--preserve=all` and `tar` needs `--acls`
choices.why: Right, and the loss is invisible until somebody is refused.

prompt: A denial persists: the bits are right, the owner is right, and `namei -l` is clean. What is worth checking next?
hint: Something above the twelve bits gets a vote.

choices.text: Whether a policy is refusing above it
choices.why: Right — mandatory access control refuses things the bits allow, root included.

choices.text: Whether the file has an access control list
choices.why: An ACL would show as a plus in the listing, which the bits check covers.

choices.text: Whether the umask is set too tightly
choices.why: A umask affects creation, and the file already exists.

choices.text: Whether the account's primary group has changed
choices.why: That would show in id, and the bits check already accounted for it.

prompt: The first search result for an SELinux denial says `setenforce 0`. What does that do?
hint: Compare it with a mode from section 57.

choices.text: Removes the one rule that refused you
choices.why: It removes none of them individually; it stops the policy being applied.

choices.text: Stops the whole policy being enforced
choices.why: Right — the chmod 777 of mandatory access control, and just as blunt.

choices.text: Puts the machine into a mode where denials are queued for review
choices.why: Permissive logs rather than queues, and setenforce 0 is how you get there — with the same loss of protection.

choices.text: Relabels the filesystem so the policy lines up with it
choices.why: That is restorecon's job, and it is usually the right fix.

prompt: Write the command that shows every access control entry on `report.txt`, including the named users.
hint: One word, then the filename.

prompt: Write `-rwxr-x---` as three octal digits.
hint: Seven, five, zero.

prompt: Write `664` as nine permission characters, without the type character.
hint: Six is read plus write.

prompt: `-rw-rw-r-- 1 ana team notes.md`. Carla is in no group named here. May she change the file?
hint: Find her row, then read it.

choices.text: Yes — the group has w and she can join it later
choices.why: Joining later is a different question from what happens now.

choices.text: No — her row is r--
choices.why: Right: the last three characters are hers, and there is no w in them.

choices.text: Yes, if she owns the directory it sits in
choices.why: Owning the directory lets her remove the name, and it does not let her edit the file.

choices.text: There is too little information to say
choices.why: Owner, group and mode are stated, and so is her membership.

prompt: `-r--rw-rw- 1 bruno team plan.md`, and bruno is in `team`. May bruno write it?
hint: Only one row is consulted.

choices.text: Yes, through the group's w
choices.why: His own row matched first, and the group's row was never reached.

choices.text: Yes, because owner rights are a superset
choices.why: There is no such rule; the rows are independent.

choices.text: No — the owner's row is r-- and it wins
choices.why: Right, and this is the trap the lesson opened with.

choices.text: It depends on the directory's mode
choices.why: The directory decides removal, and writing is decided here.

prompt: A directory is `drwxr-xr-x` and a file in it is `-rw-------`, both owned by ana. Can bruno list the directory?
hint: Listing and reading are decided in two different places.

choices.text: Yes
choices.why: Right, and he will see the name and be refused the contents.

choices.text: No — the file inside is private
choices.why: A private file does not hide its own name from a readable directory.

choices.text: Yes, but just if he is in ana's group
choices.why: The other row already grants r-x, so group membership adds nothing.

choices.text: Yes, with sudo and in no other way
choices.why: sudo would work and is not needed; the directory already allows it.

prompt: You run `chmod -R 700 ~` to tidy up your home directory. What is the most likely consequence?
hint: Think about what else reaches into a home directory.

choices.text: Nothing at all — 700 is the correct mode for a home directory
choices.why: It is right for the directory itself and wrong for everything it contains.

choices.text: Your dotfiles stop being read, because the shell needs r on them
choices.why: You keep r on your own files; the owner's row is rwx.

choices.text: The directory becomes unreadable to you as well
choices.why: You are the owner, and the owner's row is rwx.

choices.text: Every file becomes executable and ssh refuses your key
choices.why: Right: 700 on a plain file sets x, and ssh wants 600 on a private key.

prompt: Write the recursive chmod that repairs a tree where directories lost their execute bit, without making plain files executable.
hint: It uses a capital letter where you would expect a small one.

prompt: A shared directory is `drwxrwsr-x`, group `dev`. Two people work in it and keep finding each other's new files unwritable. What is missing?
hint: The bit sets the group. Something else sets the bits.

choices.text: The setgid bit, which is absent from this mode
choices.why: The s in the group slot is the setgid bit, and it is there.

choices.text: Group membership for one of the two
choices.why: Then they would not see the files at all, rather than find them unwritable.

choices.text: A umask of 002, so the group keeps its w
choices.why: Right: setgid decides the group and the umask decides the bits.

choices.text: The sticky bit, so people stop deleting each other's work
choices.why: Sticky restricts removal; the complaint here is about writing.

prompt: Which command answers `who am I, and which groups count for me` in one line?
hint: Three characters.

choices.text: whoami
choices.why: That prints the account name and stops there.

choices.text: id
choices.why: Right: uid, primary group and the whole supplementary list.

choices.text: groups
choices.why: That prints the groups and leaves out the uid.

choices.text: getent passwd
choices.why: That reads the account database and needs a name to look up.

prompt: A cron job writes a file that a colleague then cannot read. Both are in `dev`. Where do you look first?
hint: Something decided the file's mode when it was created, and it was not chmod.

choices.text: The umask the job runs under
choices.why: Right — a job started by cron or systemd carries its own, not yours.

choices.text: The colleague's supplementary groups
choices.why: Both are stated to be in dev, which is the shared group.

choices.text: The sticky bit on the directory
choices.why: Sticky governs removal, and reading is the complaint.

choices.text: The ACL mask on the file
choices.why: Worth a look if the listing shows a plus, and the mode comes first.

prompt: Put these in the order you would work through a denial you do not understand.
items: run id and read the group list
run ls -l on the file and read its row
run namei -l on the full path
check whether a policy is enforcing above the bits
trap: Identity first, then the file, then the path that reaches it.

prompt: Match each message to what it means.
hint: Two of them are about the bits and two are not.

pairs.left: carla is not in the sudoers file

right_distractors: the group list in your shell is stale
the filesystem was mounted without write access

prompt: A command needs root and writes its output into a root-owned file. Write the program that goes after the pipe so the write happens as root.
hint: Four letters, and it also prints what it wrote.

prompt: You are handed a machine and want to know what you are allowed to do before you try anything. What do you run?
hint: One command asks the rules rather than testing them.

choices.text: sudo -i, and see whether it works
choices.why: That tests it by doing it, which is the opposite of asking first.

choices.text: cat /etc/sudoers
choices.why: Reading it needs root, which is the thing in question.

choices.text: groups, and infer from the names
choices.why: Group names hint at it and the rules are what decide.

choices.text: sudo -l
choices.why: Right: it prints the rules that match you, without running any of them.

prompt: `ls -l` shows `-rw-r-----+`. What does the final character tell you?
hint: It is not part of the nine.

choices.text: The file is a symbolic link
choices.why: A link says l in the first position, not plus at the end.

choices.text: The file has one of the special bits set
choices.why: Those appear as s or t inside the nine.

choices.text: The file carries an access control list
choices.why: Right, and `getfacl` is what shows the entries.

choices.text: The mode was set with the symbolic form of chmod
choices.why: Nothing records how a mode was set.
